exercises.title: How Bees Give Directions
exercises.passage:
When a honeybee finds a good patch of flowers, she can't draw a map or point the way. Instead, she flies back to the hive and dances.

On the vertical honeycomb inside the dark hive, she runs a short straight line while shaking her body from side to side. Then she loops back around and runs the line again, over and over. Other bees crowd close and follow her movements.

The dance carries two pieces of information. The angle of the straight run tells the others which direction to fly. A run straight up the comb means "fly toward the sun." A run tilted 40 degrees to the right of straight up means "fly 40 degrees to the right of the sun." The length of the run signals distance: the longer she waggles, the farther away the flowers are.

The Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch spent decades decoding this language, and he shared the 1973 Nobel Prize for his work on animal behavior. His ideas were debated for years, but later experiments, including some using tiny robotic bees, confirmed that the dance really does guide other bees to food.
exercises.question: A bee runs a straight line tilted 40 degrees to the right of straight up, and she waggles for a long time. What is she telling the other bees?

options.text: Fly 40 degrees right of the sun; the flowers are close
Fly 40 degrees right of the sun; the flowers are far
Fly 40 degrees left of the sun; the flowers are far
Danger lies 40 degrees from the hive

mc_feedback.correct: The angle gives the direction, and the length of the waggle gives the distance.

incorrect_by_option.a: You got the direction. Now check the distance: "the longer she waggles, the farther away the flowers are."
incorrect_by_option.c: Take another look at the direction: tilted right of straight up means fly right of the sun.
incorrect_by_option.d: The dance isn't a warning. It "really does guide other bees to food."

exercises.editorial_notes: Fact-check: von Frisch shared the 1973 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine; robotic-bee experiments confirming the dance. Note sources here. SOURCES (fact-checked 2026-10-01, see docs/FACTCHECK.md): Nobel Prize 1973 press release (nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1973/press-release/); Riley et al., Nature 2005 (nature.com/articles/nature03526); Michelsen et al., Behavioral Ecology and Sociobiology 1992 (link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00166696); waggle dance reviews, PMC6835826 and PMC6955924; waggle duration and distance, PMC8029670.

exercises.title: The Spare Key
exercises.passage:
Marta had lived in the apartment on Holt Street for eleven years. Every Sunday she watered the tomato plants on the balcony, and every Sunday the man in 4B called over the railing to ask how they were coming along.

This Sunday, she stood in the doorway of the living room holding a watering can with nothing to water. The plants had gone to her niece on Thursday, along with the couch and most of the dishes. What was left fit into six boxes by the door, each labeled in thick black marker: KITCHEN, BOOKS, WINTER.

She walked down the hall to 4B and knocked. When the door opened, she held out a small brass key.

"For the new people," she said. "In case they lock themselves out. I always did, the first year."

The man turned the key over in his palm. "The balcony won't be the same," he said.

Marta laughed, but she looked at the floor when she did it. "Somebody will grow something," she said. "Somebody always does."
exercises.question: What is happening in Marta's life, and how does she seem to feel about it? Point to one detail that shows you. (1–2 sentences)

rubric.text: Infers that Marta is moving out
rubric.level_2: Clearly says she's moving or leaving

rubric.text: Infers her mixed or sad feelings
rubric.level_0: No feeling, or the wrong feeling
rubric.level_2: Names sadness she's partly hiding, or mixed feelings

rubric.text: Supports the answer with a specific detail
rubric.level_1: A detail that shows the move but not the feeling
rubric.level_2: A detail that shows the feeling (laughing while looking at the floor, the empty watering can)

anchors.label: strong
anchors.text: Marta is moving out after eleven years, and she's sadder than she lets on. She laughs, but she looks at the floor when he says the balcony won't be the same.

anchors.label: partial
anchors.text: She's moving and she's a little sad because she gave her plants away.

anchors.label: weak
anchors.text: Marta likes gardening and gets along with her neighbor.

exercises.title: The Holes That Weren't There
exercises.passage:
During the Second World War, American military analysts faced a practical problem. Bombers were being shot down at alarming rates, and armor could help, but armor is heavy. Every extra pound of steel plating cost fuel, range, and speed. Too little armor and the crews died; too much and the plane could barely fly. So the question was not whether to add armor, but where.

The planes that came back from missions seemed to offer an answer. The story, as it has been retold many times since, goes like this: analysts mapped the bullet holes on returning aircraft, and a clear pattern appeared. The wings and the body of the plane were riddled with damage. The engines, by comparison, had surprisingly few holes.

The obvious recommendation was to reinforce the areas that were being hit the most. More holes meant more danger, and more danger meant more armor.

Abraham Wald, a mathematician working with a wartime research group at Columbia University, is said to have looked at the same pattern and recommended nearly the opposite. Put the armor, he argued, where the returning planes had the fewest holes.

His reasoning has since become one of the most famous lessons in statistics, and it applies far beyond airplanes: to studies of successful companies, to advice from lottery winners, and to any conclusion drawn only from the cases that happened to survive long enough to be counted.
exercises.question: Why would Wald's recommendation make sense? Explain his reasoning in 1–2 sentences.

rubric.text: Recognizes the data came only from planes that survived
rubric.level_2: Clearly says only returning or surviving planes were studied

rubric.text: Explains what the missing holes mean
rubric.level_0: Says nothing about the areas with few holes or the damage they didn't see
rubric.level_1: Says the damage they saw wasn't what mattered, or that the missing hits mattered more, without saying those planes were lost
rubric.level_2: Says planes hit in the areas with few holes (such as the engines) were shot down or didn't make it back

rubric.text: Connects the reasoning to the armor decision
rubric.level_0: Doesn't use the words armor, protect, or reinforce (or a close synonym). An answer that only says why a part matters, such as "engines are the most important part", scores 0
rubric.level_1: Mentions armor, protecting, or reinforcing and says where it should go, but not that planes hit there didn't come back
rubric.level_2: Says the armor should go where returning planes had few holes (such as the engines), because planes hit there didn't come back

anchors.label: strong
anchors.text: They were only looking at planes that survived, so wing damage obviously wasn't fatal. Planes hit in the engines probably never came home, so that's where the armor should go.

anchors.label: partial
anchors.text: Wald realized they only studied planes that survived, so the damage they saw wasn't the damage that mattered.

anchors.label: weak
anchors.text: Because engines are the most important part of the plane.

exercises.editorial_notes: FACT-CHECK BEFORE APPROVAL. The 'engines' detail comes from popular retellings; Wald's actual memos were mathematical methods for estimating vulnerability from surviving aircraft. Keep the phrase 'as it has been retold'. Confirm Wald worked with the Statistical Research Group at Columbia. SOURCES (fact-checked 2026-10-01, see docs/FACTCHECK.md): AMS Feature Column, "The Legend of Abraham Wald" (ams.org/publicoutreach/feature-column/fc-2016-06); CNA reprint of Wald's memoranda (cna.org/analyses/1980/a-method-of-estimating-plane-vulnerability); Mangel & Samaniego, Journal of the American Statistical Association 1984.

exercises.title: The First Essays
exercises.passage:
In 1580, a French nobleman named Michel de Montaigne published a book unlike anything his readers had seen. He had stepped back from public life to a tower on his family's estate, surrounded by his library, and started writing short pieces about whatever was on his mind: friendship, fear, cannibals, sleep, lying, and his own kidney stones.

He called these pieces essais. In French, the word meant "attempts" or "trials," the way you might try out a new recipe or test a difficult climb. Montaigne wasn't claiming to have final answers. He was trying out his thinking on the page: changing his mind in the middle, contradicting himself, and admitting what he didn't know. "What do I know?" became his personal motto.

The word stuck. Today, "essay" usually means a school assignment with a thesis statement and five tidy paragraphs. But the original idea was looser and braver. Writing was a way of discovering what you think, not just reporting what you had already decided.
exercises.question: A friend of yours hates writing essays. In 1–2 sentences, explain why Montaigne's idea of an essay might change how they feel about it.

rubric.text: Conveys the core idea: an essay as an attempt, writing to explore rather than to prove
rubric.level_1: Mentions "attempt" without what it means for writing
rubric.level_2: Explains that you write to figure out what you think

rubric.text: Speaks to the friend: why this would feel different
rubric.level_0: Gives the friend no reason to feel differently
rubric.level_1: General reassurance not tied to how writing works, such as "it doesn't have to be perfect" or "it's easier"
rubric.level_2: Names a relief that comes from Montaigne's idea: you don't need your opinion worked out before you start, or you can change your mind as you write

rubric.text: Puts the ideas in the writer's own words
rubric.level_0: Only restates facts from the passage (names, dates, places, details of the story or experiment), or copies a whole sentence from it
rubric.level_1: Copies a run of 5 or more words in a row from the passage
rubric.level_2: No run of 5 or more words is copied from the passage. Shared single words or short phrases (such as "attempt", "meant", "fool", "brain") don't count as copying. Paraphrasing a fact from the passage is fine. A short answer can earn this

anchors.label: strong
anchors.text: Montaigne's essays were just attempts. He wrote to figure out what he thought, changing his mind as he went. So you don't need the answer before you start; writing is how you get there.

anchors.label: partial
anchors.text: An essay originally meant an attempt, so it doesn't have to be perfect.

anchors.label: weak
anchors.text: Montaigne wrote about cannibals and kidney stones in 1580.

exercises.editorial_notes: Fact-check: Essais first published 1580; motto 'Que sais-je?'; the tower (library) on the family estate. SOURCES (fact-checked 2026-10-01, see docs/FACTCHECK.md): Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Michel de Montaigne" (plato.stanford.edu/entries/montaigne/); The Montaigne Project, 1580 edition, Books I and II (lib.uchicago.edu/efts/ARTFL/projects/montaigne/1580essais1.html and 1580essais2.html).

exercises.title: Two Clinics
exercises.passage:
In the 1840s, Vienna General Hospital ran two maternity clinics side by side. Women were admitted to one or the other on alternating days, so the two groups of patients were broadly similar. Their fates were not. In the First Clinic, staffed by doctors and medical students, a disease called childbed fever killed mothers at a far higher rate than in the Second Clinic, staffed by midwives. In some years the gap was so well known that women begged not to be sent to the First Clinic.

Ignaz Semmelweis, a young Hungarian doctor working in the First Clinic, set out to find the difference. He ruled out explanations one by one. Crowding was actually worse in the Second Clinic, because women avoided the First. He had doctors copy the midwives' delivery position. He even changed the route the priest took when bringing last rites to dying patients, in case fear was the cause. Nothing changed.

Then, in 1847, a colleague named Jakob Kolletschka died after being cut by a student's scalpel during an autopsy. His illness looked strikingly like childbed fever. Semmelweis also knew something about the First Clinic's daily routine: its doctors and students often came to the maternity ward straight from dissecting bodies in the autopsy room. The midwives did not perform autopsies.

Semmelweis ordered everyone in the First Clinic to wash their hands in a chlorinated lime solution before examining patients. Within months, the death rate fell to roughly the level of the Second Clinic.
exercises.question: Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?

options.text: The midwives were simply more skilled at delivering babies
Doctors were carrying something from the dead bodies to the mothers on their hands
Crowded wards made childbed fever less likely
Fear of the priest's visits was making mothers sick

mc_feedback.correct: Three clues point the same way: Kolletschka's illness, the autopsy routine, and what happened after handwashing.

incorrect_by_option.a: The passage never compares skill, and handwashing alone closed the gap.
incorrect_by_option.c: Crowding was actually worse in the Second Clinic, which is how Semmelweis ruled it out.
incorrect_by_option.d: Semmelweis tested that one. He changed the priest's route and nothing changed.

exercises.editorial_notes: FACT-CHECK BEFORE APPROVAL: mortality comparison between clinics, Kolletschka's death in 1847, timing of the chlorinated-lime handwashing order. Keep figures qualitative unless a source is cited. SOURCES (fact-checked 2026-10-01, see docs/FACTCHECK.md): James Lind Library (jameslindlibrary.org/articles/ignaz-phillip-semmelweis-studies-of-death-in-childbirth/); Noakes et al., Epidemiology & Infection 2008 (cambridge.org, "Semmelweis and the aetiology of puerperal sepsis 160 years on"); GMS Hygiene and Infection Control, "Ignaz Philipp Semmelweis (1818-1865)" (journals.publisso.de/en/journals/hic/volume20/dgkh000608); Carl Hempel, Philosophy of Natural Science (1966), ch. 2.
